newsitem.title: USA: N.Y. transit union says contractors are too costly.
newsitem.headline: N.Y. transit union says contractors are too costly.

text.p: New York transit workers urged the Metropolitan Transportation Authority on Tuesday to expand its construction workforce, saying lax oversight caused the state agency to waste money on contractors.

The proposal was made by Arthur Goldberg, a representative of the Transport Union Workers Local 100, at a meeting of the agency's capital program oversight committee. It runs counter to privatization efforts now under way at several state agencies.

"Today we proposed an expansion of the in-house workforce and the creation of a dedicated capital construction workforce so that they would save money and improve on oversight and stay on schedule," Goldberg said in a telephone interview.
The union official, who said that he hoped the MTA would respond later, added that he detected a lot of interest in the plan. A spokesman for the authority was not immediately available to comment.

At the committee meeting, Goldberg said questions were raised about a two-year, $174 million overhaul of Grand Central Station in midtown Manhattan. With 26 percent of the work completed, the contractor already spent $45 million, suggesting a budget overrun was possible. The railway terminal project was scheduled to be completed in December 1997.
"There were concerns because of the possiblity of it continuing to expand....It could go into many millions of dollars," Goldberg said.
He said similar concerns have arisen over a $60 million project to renovate Union Square, which is located at 14th Street in lower Manhattan.

Goldberg said that in the authority's report on 1995 construction, it said that about 36 jobs being carried out by contractors were 16 percent over budget, with four of these projects exceeding their budgets by 10 percent.
Saying union workers had proved more accountable, Goldberg said they were under budget in 1995 on every one of the four to five projects they were assigned.
For example, a $10 million renovation of the Broad Street subway station in downtown Manhattan was $1 million under budget, Goldberg said, citing the authority's report.
With a similar effort at a midtown subway stop located across from the Plaza Hotel, "we're months ahead of schedule and several hundreds of thousands of dollars under budget," he said.
